title: Wisconsin Infant Dies of Measles, State's First Such Death Since 1990
excerpt: The infant, in southwestern Wisconsin, was linked to an outbreak that has reached 431 cases in 13 counties — the state's highest count in more than 35 years, health officials said.
body:
• An infant in southwestern Wisconsin has died of measles, the first such death reported in the state since 1990, the Wisconsin Department of Health Services said on November 5; the coroner listed measles as the immediate cause of death.
  • Wisconsin has reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties so far in 2026, its highest count in more than 35 years, with nine people hospitalised for severe symptoms.
  • The Grant County health officer said the infant was too young to be vaccinated, according to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel.
  • For readers: check your family's MMR status in the Wisconsin Immunization Registry or through your health care provider — two doses are about 97% effective at preventing measles, DHS said.

An infant in southwestern Wisconsin has died after contracting measles, the Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS) announced on Thursday, November 5. It is the first death of its kind reported in the state since 1990 — 36 years ago. The coroner listed the immediate cause of death as measles, and DHS said it would not release any additional information about the child or the family to protect their privacy.

"Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease."

— Kirsten Johnson, Wisconsin DHS Secretary

An outbreak at a 35-year high

The death is connected to the ongoing outbreak in southwestern Wisconsin. As of November 3, DHS had reported 431 measles cases across 13 counties in 2026, the highest number seen in the state in more than 35 years, up from 335 cases two weeks earlier, according to CIDRAP at the University of Minnesota. Nine people have required hospitalisation for severe symptoms. DHS cautioned that reported counts may not reflect the full extent of spread, because not everyone who becomes ill seeks medical care or gets tested.

The Grant County health officer said the infant was too young to be vaccinated, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported. On November 3, the state health department recommended that babies six months and older who are likely to be exposed to measles receive an early dose, and between 500 and 600 such doses have been given to Wisconsin infants since August, DHS immunisation programme manager Stephanie Schauer said in a November 5 media briefing, according to the Journal Sentinel.

The third US death reported this week

The Wisconsin death was the third measles-related death reported by a US state health department this week, after an infant in New York and a person in Pennsylvania, CIDRAP reported. At least eight people have died in the United States this year from measles complications, according to state reports, while the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention added one death to its official toll this week, bringing that total to four — a gap CIDRAP attributed to the CDC no longer automatically adding deaths confirmed by state officials. The CDC count put total US cases this year at 4,852.

What DHS is doing, and what residents should do

DHS said it is working with local and Tribal health departments on case identification, testing and vaccination. Since August 1, it has delivered 2,000 doses of MMR vaccine to local health departments in communities with confirmed cases, and more than 42,000 doses have been administered by health care providers in Wisconsin in that time.

Measles can cause life-threatening complications including pneumonia and swelling of the brain, and children younger than five, pregnant people and people with weakened immune systems are at increased risk, DHS said. The department advises anyone exposed to measles to stay home, and anyone who develops fever and a rash to contact their health care provider and call ahead before visiting a clinic or hospital so steps can be taken to avoid exposing others. Wisconsin residents can check their vaccination records through the Wisconsin Immunization Registry or through their provider or local health department.
